name: Snowshill Manor

dates.altered: The listed-building entry records 'C17, c1720, C19, altered 1919-23 by and for C.P. Wade; minor later alterations'. The registered park and garden entry adds that the earliest part is 'the north hall of c 1500, converted to two storeys in c 1600' and that 'In 1712, William Sanbach altered the south end and added a projecting room to the west to give a classical front.'
dates.note: THREE DATINGS ARE ON RECORD AND NONE IS RESOLVED HERE. The node's exemplar gives the year 1500 and calls the house 'late medieval and Tudor ... refronted around 1720'. Historic England's listed-building entry 1340081 begins the building at C17. Historic England's own registered park and garden entry 1000781 begins it at 'the north hall of c 1500' and dates the classical front to 1712 rather than c1720. Two Historic England entries for one house disagree with each other about both ends of its history.

refs.title: Snowshill Manor
refs.note: The registered park and garden, whose PRINCIPAL BUILDING paragraph describes the house independently of the listed-building entry and is the only source read here that states its plan and storey count in one sentence: 'Snowshill Manor (listed grade II\) is a Z-plan house of two-and-a-half storeys, built of coursed, squared Cotswold stone with stone slate roofs.' Read as continuous prose in an extract.

survey.prepared: The Details section's legacy header carries the date 4.7.60 (4 July 1960). No Official list entry block was returned by either extract of this page; a planning.data.gov.uk row for the same reference prints 'start-date: 1960-07-04' and 'entry-date: 1987-09-07', which corroborates the first date and is not the entry's own statement.

measurements.note: Worth carrying because the node's own prose says a Cotswold house sits with 'a hard, clean edge against the sky' and says nothing about how far it stands above grade; three steps is the only figure any source here gives for that.

measurements.note: The eighteenth-century refronting the node's exemplar note names. An 18-pane sash is a six-over-nine or nine-over-nine, and the entry does not say which.

note: Tranche 3, the English cottage and the Cotswold vernacular, 5 Sep 2026. TWO HISTORIC ENGLAND ENTRIES FOR ONE HOUSE DISAGREE ABOUT ITS DATE, and both are carried. The house is the node's own demonstration case -- Georgian fashion absorbed without changing material or roof -- and the entry shows it in one sentence: mullion-and-transom windows to the right of the door and sashes to its left, across a 'change in stone colour'. A QUOTE THAT STRADDLED TWO EXTRACT CHUNKS WAS FOUND BY RE-EXTRACTING THE PAGE WITH A DIFFERENT QUERY AND WAS SPLIT RATHER THAN JOINED. The chunker returns the same boundaries on every query and each block repeats the tail of the one before, so the text is demonstrably continuous -- but a span crossing the boundary was never READ as one contiguous run, and this record does not print one as though it had been.
